title: Stretching Short Sequences of DNA with Constant Force Axial Optical Tweezers
protocol: Split the beam from a 1064 nm laser into two orthogonally polarized beams.
Use one beam for manipulating the biomolecule and the other for calibration.
Control the intensity of the manipulation beam with an acousto-optic deflector (AOD).
Independently control the position and focus of each beam using beam steering mirrors and optical telescopes.
Recombine the beams with a polarizing beam splitter.
Condition the recombined beams further by a set of telescoping optics to slightly overfill the back aperture of the microscope objective.
Ensure the calibration beam is overfilled by 50% for a tight optical trap.
Adjust the manipulation beam to be approximately 20% overfilled for a larger workable region of the linear potential.
Tightly focus both beams onto the sample cell using a PlanApo 60x/1.4 oil immersion microscope objective.
Load a sample chamber with a disperse solution of 800 nm diameter polystyrene microspheres diluted in phosphate buffered saline.
Let the sample sit for 10-15 minutes and then lightly flush with buffer to remove excess microspheres.
Locate a randomly stuck microsphere on the coverglass.
Adjust the height of the sample chamber until the microsphere is approximately 1 μm below the focus.
Find the centre of the microsphere using the geometric pattern matching function in LabView.
Generate a radial intensity profile of the microsphere by averaging 360° about the center of each cross section.
Fit the radial profile with a quadratic function to find a brightness peak.
Measure the distance between this peak and the center as the apparent size of the bead.
Gradually increase the axial position of the microsphere using the calibrated piezostage.
Acquire an image at each axial position with the CCD camera.
Repeat image analysis for each successive image to correlate the apparent size of the bead with its axial location.
Collinearly align the manipulation beam and the calibration beam.
Set the calibration beam to around 50 mW at the back aperture of the objective.
Adjust the manipulation beam to a much weaker power, say 10 mW.
With the manipulation beam switched off, confine a free microsphere within the stiffer trap of the calibration beam.
Turn on the manipulation beam.
Shift the axial focus of the calibration beam by adjusting the telescopic lens while keeping the microsphere trapped in the calibration beam.
Measure the subsequent displacement of the microsphere after turning on the manipulation beam and repeat the process.
Plot the displacements ΔX against the axial position of the focus of the calibration beam.
Move the microsphere, trapped by the calibration beam, to around a micrometer above the surface by adjusting the telescopic lens while switching off the manipulation beam.
Record the thermal axial motion of the microsphere by measuring the intensity of transmitted light with a photodetector.
Mount the chamber containing surface tethered DNA molecules and adjust the focus of the manipulation beam slightly above the unstretched microspheres by adjusting the telescope.
Adjust the position of the stage until one of the microspheres is trapped.
Roughly position the microsphere in the center of the XY plane of the optical trap.
Generate a series of square waves in LabView and send them to the AOD to repetitively turn the laser beam on and off.
Control the intensity of the laser and the duration of the on state to prevent heating of the sample chamber.
Use around 2 mW of laser power (measured at the back aperture of the objective) and send pulses of 200 ms (on) and 500 ms (off).
Set the amplitude of the square wave sent to the AOD to be around 0.5 V.
Watch the microsphere as the trap is repeatedly turned on and off.
Note if the laser induces any preferential direction to the microsphere's motion.
Iteratively adjust the microsphere position in both the X and Y directions by controlling the piezostage.
Ensure the random motion of the microsphere becomes isotropic in the XY plane.
Restrict the microsphere's motion when the laser is on.
Align the bead in the Z direction.
Pulse the laser beam on and off while simultaneously measuring the microsphere's axial displacement in real time.
Center the stage within the linear region, which is the point where the Z displacement is greatest.
Check that the trap is centered in the XY plane after careful alignment in the Z direction.
Repeat both the XY and Z alignment if the XY alignment has changed until the microsphere is centered properly along all three axes.
Ramp the laser intensity by sending a voltage signal to the AOD from 0 V to 0.5 V in steps of 0.025 V.
Record 400 frames at 100 fps and average them to obtain the axial displacement in each step.
Plot force extension curves and fit them to a modified WLC model.
